subtype: Approach: making saving visible with a chart [Action]
passage:
“Bhavna, what is that red tube on your wall?” Mummy asked.
“A savings thermometer. The top is 3,000 for the camera, and each section is 250. See? I coloured the first two.”
“You could just check your tin.”
“The tin is boring. I need to see it going up. Last week I wanted earrings, and then I looked at the wall and thought, that's one box I won't colour.”
“So it's working?”
“Two boxes done, ten to go. I skipped pizza tonight, and my hand is itching to colour box three.”
From the kitchen Papa called, “Jaya, is the dal ready?” Mummy laughed. “Give me the red pen. I'll hold the tape.”

qa.q: How much is each section of the thermometer worth?
What does Bhavna feel when she wants earrings and looks at the wall?
qa.a: She feels tempted but determined, because the thought of one box she won't colour keeps her going.

qa.q: What could Bhavna do if the chart stops motivating her?
qa.a: She could add a small reward at each milestone or tell the family so they can cheer her on, since visible progress helps through dull weeks.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the thermometer?
qa.a: Mummy seems amused and supportive, since she asks for the pen and offers to hold the tape, and she sees her daughter's effort.

grounding: A teen draws a savings thermometer on her wall and colours it each week, and seeing it fill keeps her saving through tempting weeks.

subtype: Approach: making saving visible with a chart [Action]
passage:
The thermometer is still on my wall, even though the camera was bought long ago. I'm Kalyani, and I drew it the day I decided to save for a secondhand camera: a tall red bulb on chart paper, with lines from zero at the bottom to the full amount at the top, one line for each week's saving.
Every Sunday night I coloured one line red. That was it. But it worked in a way I didn't expect. In weeks when everyone was going to the new ice-cream place, or when Irawati wanted to go to the mall, I'd look at the half-red thermometer and think, I don't want an empty line this week. Sometimes I went anyway and just had water. Twice I skipped.
Around week fifteen the red passed the halfway mark, and I actually cheered. By week twenty-eight the red touched the top.
Irawati says it's childish. She's drawing one now too.

qa.q: What did Kalyani do every Sunday night?
How did Kalyani feel when the red passed halfway?
qa.a: Kalyani felt excited and proud enough to actually cheer.

qa.q: What else could Kalyani add to keep the chart motivating?
qa.a: Small marks for milestones, like a sticker at each quarter, so the long middle weeks feel rewarding too.

qa.q: How does Irawati see the thermometer?
qa.a: Irawati calls it childish, yet is drawing one too, which suggests quiet admiration.

grounding: Shows a teen drawing a savings thermometer and colouring it weekly, and how seeing it fill keeps her going when spending feels more fun.

subtype: Approach: making saving visible with a chart [Action]
passage:
Class teacher's note, money-skills project, week twelve
When the class began the saving project, most students kept their totals in a notebook and forgot about them. Kiran did something different. She drew a large thermometer on chart paper and taped it inside her locker door, with the goal, a set of watercolours and brushes, written at the top.
Every Monday she coloured in the week's saving. I noticed that in the weeks after the school fête and the book fair, when others spent everything, her thermometer still went up, just by a smaller amount. When I asked how, she said, “I didn't want a gap in it. It looks sad.”
Her younger sister Yamini, in Class Six, has started coming to the locker to see it.
This week the red reached the top. Kiran showed me the paints before assembly. I will ask her to share the idea with the class.

qa.q: Where did Kiran tape the thermometer?
What does Kiran's answer "It looks sad" reveal?
qa.a: It shows she felt attached to the chart and would be disappointed to leave a gap, which kept her saving in tempting weeks.

qa.q: How could the class use Kiran's idea?
qa.a: Each student could draw a visible chart for their own goal, so progress is seen every week instead of forgotten in a notebook.

qa.q: What might the thermometer mean to Yamini?
qa.a: Yamini seems curious and impressed, visiting the locker, and may be picking up the habit by watching.

grounding: A teacher notes a teen whose weekly-coloured savings thermometer keeps her saving through fête and book-fair weeks until the goal is reached.
